paraphrase: Prakaraṇa 4 (Alātaśānti, "the quenching of the firebrand"), verses 4.1–4.100. Movements: (4.1–4.2) salutations to the one who knew the dharmas as sky-like and to asparśa-yoga; (4.3–4.10) disputants who hold birth of the existent or of the non-existent each proclaim non-birth; the immortal cannot become mortal; the nature that does not change; (4.11–4.23) a critique of cause and effect (which is first? sequence, simultaneity, seed and sprout), concluding that nothing is born from itself or from another, nor as existent, non-existent or both (4.22); (4.24–4.30) the vocabulary of designation, sign and object; mind does not touch objects and is not born; saṃsāra and liberation not ended or endless; (4.31–4.41) dream and waking argued to be alike unreal, as at prakaraṇa 2; (4.42–4.46) birth was taught to those afraid of non-birth; consciousness unborn, motionless and non-dual; (4.47–4.53) the firebrand: appearances of straight and crooked are the motion of the firebrand; likewise appearances of grasped and grasper are the vibration of consciousness; they come from nowhere; (4.54–4.60) dharmas and mind not born of each other; saṃsāra lasts while absorption in cause and effect lasts; by convention born, in true being unborn; māyā-seed and sprout; (4.61–4.72) dream and waking mind vibrating as dual by māyā; jīvas as dream-made, māyā-made or conjured exist and do not exist; no jīva is born; (4.73–4.81) imagined and dependent conventions; adherence to the unreal; the signless mind not born; the state dawning of itself, once-shone; (4.82–4.86) the four positions by which the Lord is covered; omniscience and peace; (4.87–4.90) worldly duality with and without object, beyond-the-world without object or apprehension; the threefold knowledge; (4.91–4.99) all dharmas awakened, peaceful, pure and equal from the beginning; those who see difference are wretched; knowledge unattached; (4.100) closing salutation to the unborn state.

paraphrase: Thesis of the Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda), decided from the six marks of purport. The text teaches that nothing is born (ajāti): all dharmas and all jīvas are unborn, and duality is the appearing of mind through māyā, as in dream; the one self is threefold (viśva, taijasa, prājña) and its fourth (turya) is non-dual, unborn, sleepless and dreamless (1.1, 1.10–1.16, 2.32, 3.48, 4.71, 4.81). Opening and closing (upakrama-upasaṃhāra): it opens by restating the Upaniṣad's three and the fourth (1.1) and closes with a salutation to the unborn state, hard to see, very deep, of sameness, without multiplicity (4.100), after salutations at 4.1–4.2. Repetition (abhyāsa): non-birth is declared in each prakaraṇa (1.16–1.17, 2.32, 3.2, 3.19–3.28, 3.48, 4.4, 4.22, 4.71); the dream-waking argument returns (2.1–2.10 and 4.31–4.41, 4.61–4.67); and several verses recur nearly word for word (2.6 = 4.31; 2.7 = 4.32; 3.20–3.22 = 4.6–4.8; 3.29–3.30 = 4.61–4.62; 3.48 = 4.71). Novelty (apūrvatā): the text argues non-origination by reasoning in the manner of a treatise (4.11–4.23), gives the images of pot-space (3.3–3.9), the rope (2.17–2.18) and the firebrand (4.47–4.52), names asparśa-yoga (3.39, 4.2) and gives a counsel for the mind in restraint (3.40–3.46). Stated result (phala): fearlessness, ending of sorrow, awakening and imperishable peace depend on restraint of the mind (3.40); one who knows Oṃ is a muni (1.29) and does not grieve (1.28); the state free of sorrow, desire and fear (4.78); fitness for immortality (4.92); omniscience (4.85, 4.89). Praise (arthavāda): the honouring of the knower of the common feature of the three stations (1.22) and of those ascertained in the unborn sameness (4.95) are in the form of praise. Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): the unreality of dream and waking from dream itself (2.1–2.10), the immortal cannot become mortal (3.19–3.22, 4.6–4.8), the denial of birth from itself or another and as existent, non-existent or both (4.22) and the critique of cause and effect (4.11–4.21). The text also speaks at the practical level: worship taught out of compassion for the three kinds of āśrama (3.16), yoking the mind to Oṃ (1.25), fixing memory on non-duality (2.36), and the counsel on laya, distraction, kaṣāya and relishing of happiness (3.42–3.45). Main teaching: non-birth, taught from the ultimate standpoint (2.32), with the conventional teaching of birth given as a means (3.15, 4.42) and the practical counsel kept alongside it.
